hints: Think about the two structures every virus must have to work: its genetic material inside and its protein coat outside. What are they made from?
Recall which bond holds nucleotides together in DNA or RNA, which bond holds amino acids together in proteins, and what larger family both of these bonds belong to.
walkthrough:
**Recall what ALL viruses contain**

All viruses have two essential parts. They have nucleic acid (either DNA or RNA) as their genome, and they have a protein capsid coat around it.

So ask yourself: what bonds hold nucleic acids together, and what bonds hold proteins together?

**Match parts to bonds 1 and 2**

Nucleic acids are polynucleotides. Adjacent nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds. So 1 is present in all viruses.

Proteins are polypeptides. Adjacent amino acids are joined by peptide bonds. So 2 is present in all viruses.

**Check bond 3**

This is the clever part. Both phosphodiester bonds and peptide bonds involve sharing of electrons between atoms.

That means they are both examples of covalent bonds. So if 1 and 2 are present, 3 must also be present. That gives 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. All viruses have nucleic acid (phosphodiester bonds) and protein (peptide bonds), and both are types of covalent bond.
options.B: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 2 but misses that phosphodiester and peptide bonds are both covalent, so 3 is also true.
options.C: Not quite. It misses 2. All viruses have a protein capsid, so peptide bonds must be present in all viruses.
options.D: Not quite. It misses 1. All viruses have DNA or RNA, so phosphodiester bonds must be present in all viruses.
